bonds.title: The philosophy student
bonds.busy: Seminar. Well, lunch, then seminar. I'm at the bridge in the daytime and the early evening.

ranks.title: The path's name
ranks.invite: You're walking slowly. That's the correct speed here. Got a bit of the {slot}? I'll give you the short lecture.
talk: Nishida Kitaro taught philosophy at Kyoto University from 1910, and walked along this canal to think. His students followed, and their students. So: the Philosopher's Path.
The name only became official in 1972, when the neighbours tidied the path and asked the city. Before that it was just the way along the canal.
ranks.fact: The Philosopher's Path is named for Nishida Kitaro, who taught at Kyoto University from 1910 and walked the canal to think; the name was made official in 1972.

ask.q: What do you think he was thinking about?

options.reply: That's almost his actual answer. He called it pure experience: before you split the world into you and it. Also, probably, lunch.
Bigger and smaller than that. He called it pure experience: the moment before you sort the world into you and it.

request.text: Walk down to Honen-in's thatched gate
request.ask: Have you been down as far as Honen-in? A few minutes off the path, up some mossy steps. Go and stand in the gate.

ranks.title: White sand
talk: You saw the two beds of sand inside the gate? You walk between them to be made clean. The monks rake a new pattern every few days: water, leaves, whatever the season is.
The novelist Tanizaki is buried up behind it. He chose the spot himself. Good taste to the end.
ranks.fact: Inside Honen-in's thatched gate lie the byakusadan, two raised beds of white sand raked with seasonal patterns; the novelist Tanizaki Jun'ichiro is buried in the temple's graveyard.

gives.name: Seminar snacks
gives.text: Taste: you know where a student eats well

request.text: Sit down with something sweet by the canal
request.ask: Have you had the warabi mochi yet? Philosophy is impossible without sugar.

ranks.title: The stone
talk: Good. Now you can think.
Partway down, by a little bridge, there's a stone with Nishida's poem on it. 'Others are others, I am myself; come what may, I go the way I go.'
It went up in 1981. Every student in my department has been photographed beside it looking serious. I have. It's on my mother's fridge.
ranks.fact: A stone beside the path, set up in 1981, carries Nishida Kitaro's poem: 'Others are others, I am myself; come what may, I go the way I go.'

ask.q: Is that a brave poem or a stubborn one?

options.reply: A-plus. My professor took forty minutes to say that.
Half marks. He was, famously. But he'd buried a wife and children by then. I'd call it brave too.

request.text: Go up the lane to Ginkaku-ji
request.ask: Have you been up to Ginkaku-ji yet? It's at the top of the lane behind me. Go and see whether it's silver.

ranks.title: Not silver
talk: So. Was it silver?
It never was. Yoshimasa, the shogun who built it in the 1480s, died before it was finished, and nobody is sure he ever meant to. The name came later, to match the gold one across town.
What he did finish is the taste: bare wood, a cone of sand to catch the moon, a room of four and a half mats. Half of what we call Japanese started in that garden.
ranks.fact: Ginkaku-ji, the Silver Pavilion, was begun by the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa in 1482 and was never covered in silver; its Togu-do holds the Dojinsai, a four-and-a-half-mat room seen as the origin of the tea room.

gives.name: A student's rates
gives.text: 15% more for every job along the path

request.text: Show the lost half of a tour group the way
request.ask: There are always people on the path holding a map upside down. Help some: it's in your diary, under Work.

ranks.title: The way I go
talk: I heard. You pointed a whole tour group at Nanzen-ji and they went. Power.
I graduate in March and I still don't know what philosophy is for. But I know this path at every hour, and which cat owns which bench.
That might be the same thing. Come back in April. You won't see the water for petals.
ranks.fact: The Philosopher's Path runs about 2 km along a branch of the Lake Biwa Canal, from the bridge below Ginkaku-ji south to Nyakuoji.

gives.name: Pure experience
gives.text: Bearings, from someone who walks it daily

bonds.title: The canal keeper
bonds.busy: I walk the water first thing. Find me here in the mornings; after that I'm asleep or at the bathhouse.

ranks.title: Water that runs north
ranks.invite: You're looking at the water. Good. Most look at the cherries. Have you some of the {slot}? I'll show you a thing about it.
talk: Drop a leaf in. See which way it goes? North. Every river in Kyoto runs south, and this runs north, towards Ginkaku-ji.
It isn't a river. It's a branch of the Lake Biwa Canal, laid along the foot of the hills so level that the lake's own height pushes it along.
ranks.fact: The canal beside the Philosopher's Path is a branch of the Lake Biwa Canal and flows north, against the southward run of Kyoto's rivers.

ask.q: Why would they send it north, do you think?

options.text: To water the north of the city
options.reply: That's it. Fields, mills and garden ponds up the east side, where no river reached. They followed the line of the hill to get there.
Ha. No. They wanted water for the north-east: fields, mills, gardens. They followed the line of the hill.

request.text: Follow the water back to the Keage Incline
request.ask: Have you been down to Keage yet? That's where it all comes out of the mountain.

ranks.title: A man of twenty-one
talk: So you've seen where it arrives. The tunnel from the lake comes out just above there.
The engineer was Tanabe Sakuro. He was twenty-one when they gave him the job, straight out of college, and there were no foreign engineers on it. That was new, in the 1880s.
It opened in 1890, and the Emperor came. Now: my old log book is due back at the office at Keage, and my knees aren't. It's paid.
ranks.fact: The Lake Biwa Canal, completed in 1890, was designed by Tanabe Sakuro, appointed its chief engineer at 21, and built without foreign engineers.

gives.name: The keeper's legs
gives.text: A paid errand along the canal, in your diary under Work

request.text: Take the keeper's log book to Keage
request.ask: The log book's wrapped in oilcloth on the bench. It's in your diary, under Work.

ranks.title: Lake water, running downhill
talk: They got the book? Good. Years I carried that myself.

Halfway through the digging, Tanabe went to America, saw a power station driven by water in Colorado, and came home and changed the plan. Keage got its own in 1891, the first in Japan to sell power to a city.
Four years on, Kyoto ran Japan's first electric tram on it. All from lake water running downhill.
ranks.fact: Keage Power Station, fed by the Lake Biwa Canal, began in 1891 as Japan's first hydroelectric station for public supply, and in 1895 powered the country's first electric tram, in Kyoto.

ask.q: What do you reckon it does today?

options.reply: Both. The station still turns, and nearly all of Kyoto's tap water comes down that tunnel. People think it's a museum piece.
The cherries get the credit. But that's Kyoto's tap water, nearly all of it, and the station still turns.

request.text: Guess a building's height to within a quarter (G)
request.ask: Try your eye on Nanzen-ji's big gate: press G and guess its height. Then I'll tell you about the bridge behind it.

ranks.title: The brick bridge
talk: Twenty-two metres, the gate. You weren't far off.
Behind it my water crosses the temple grounds on a brick aqueduct, ninety-three metres long, built in 1888. Brick arches in a Zen temple. There was a row.
They made it arches on purpose, so that it would sit quietly among old things. A hundred and thirty years on, visitors photograph it more than the garden.
ranks.fact: The Suirokaku aqueduct, built in 1888, carries the canal's branch across Nanzen-ji's grounds on brick arches 93.2 m long.

gives.name: A level eye
gives.text: Eye: you judge a level like a canal man

request.text: Stand under the aqueduct in the morning, before the crowds
request.ask: Go and stand under the arches early, when it's only you and the drip. Then come and tell me it isn't handsome.

ranks.title: The screens
talk: Well? I said so.
Most of my working life was raking leaves off the screens so that the water kept moving. Nobody photographs a screen. But stop for a week and there's no petals drifting north, no fireflies, no path.
Somebody does it still. Nod to them if you pass. That's all a keeper wants.
ranks.fact: Genji fireflies breed along the canal beside the Philosopher's Path and fly from late May to mid-June; they are a registered natural monument of Kyoto City.

gives.name: The keeper's nod
gives.text: Bearings, from a man who walked the water daily

bonds.title: The photographer on the incline
bonds.busy: Shh, I'm waiting for a cloud to move. I'm on the rails early and late, in dry weather. The middle of the day is no use to me.

ranks.title: Rails with no trains
ranks.invite: You're walking on the sleepers, not beside them. One of us. Have you a little of the {slot}?
talk: These rails never carried a train. They carried boats. A canal boat floated onto a cradle at the top, and a cable let it down the slope, five hundred and eighty-two metres, to the water at the bottom.
It ran from 1891 to 1948. Then lorries won, and it sat rusting until someone noticed how the cherries met over it.
ranks.fact: The Keage Incline carried canal boats on wheeled cradles over a 582 m slope between two levels of the Lake Biwa Canal, from 1891 until 1948.

ask.q: Where would you put the camera?

options.reply: Yes! Down on the sleepers, rails running away to a point. Everyone else shoots standing up and gets the backs of heads.
You get the tops of heads that way. Get down between the rails and let them run to a point.

request.text: Photograph the incline's rails (photo mode, O)
request.ask: Go on, then. Low, between the rails. Photo mode. Show me when you've got it.

ranks.title: The boat on its cradle
talk: Low and straight. Good.
The boat sitting on its cradle down the slope is a copy, put there so people understand. The real ones carried rice, charcoal and timber between the lake and the city.
Here, give me your camera. I shoot dusk on slow film: deep blue, warm lamps. I've set yours the same way.
ranks.fact: A restored cradle with a replica cargo boat stands on the Keage Incline's rails, which are laid about 2.5 m apart to carry a boat.

gives.name: Dusk film
gives.text: Photographs after sunset come out on Sumire's slow film: deep blue, warm lamps

request.text: Take one photograph at golden or blue hour (photo mode, O)
request.ask: Now use it. One frame at the end of the day, when the rails go gold and then blue.

ranks.title: Ninety cherries
talk: That's the light. You waited for it.
There are about ninety cherry trees along here, Somei-Yoshino mostly. For ten days in spring you can't see a sleeper for people. I come at five in the morning then.
The rest of the year it's mine. Autumn is better anyway: nobody has told the tour buses.
ranks.fact: About 90 cherry trees, mostly Somei-Yoshino, line the Keage Incline and flower from late March to early April.

options.text: At dawn, in the first week of April
options.reply: And you'd find me already here, and I'd pretend not to mind.
With four thousand friends. Dawn, first week of April. Trust me.

request.ask: I've put a list in your diary, under Work: the gate, the aqueduct, the rails. A magazine wants them and I've only two hands.

ranks.title: What a view
talk: The editor thinks I took them. I'll confess eventually.
You shot the Sanmon. In the kabuki play, the outlaw Goemon sits up on its balcony with a pipe and says 'What a view, what a view.' Everyone in Japan knows the line.
The gate was built in 1628. Goemon was boiled alive in 1594. The view is real, though. You can pay and go up.
ranks.fact: Nanzen-ji's Sanmon gate, 22 m high, was built in 1628 by Todo Takatora; the kabuki scene in which the outlaw Ishikawa Goemon admires the view from it is set decades before the gate existed.

gives.name: A photographer's credit
gives.text: 25% more for every job along the path

request.ask: Keep shooting at the ends of the day. When you stop checking the screen after every frame, come back.

ranks.title: One frame
talk: You've stopped looking at the screen. Good.
My favourite picture of this place has no cherries in it. February, wet rails, one old man walking up the middle with his shopping. I waited four winters for him.
Leave the rails as you found them. Somebody else is waiting for you to walk through their frame.
ranks.fact: The Keage Incline and the other works of the Lake Biwa Canal were designated a National Historic Site in 1996.

gives.name: Four winters
gives.text: Light, from someone who waits for it

jobs.title: Which way from the path?
jobs.blurb: Half a tour group has lost the other half. Face each place's true bearing; the nearer, the better the pay.
jobs.who: The lost half of a tour group

jobs.title: The gate, the water, the rails
jobs.blurb: A magazine wants Nanzen-ji's Sanmon, the brick aqueduct and the Keage Incline. Photo mode (O); golden or blue hour pays a quarter more.
jobs.done: Sumire looks at them for a long time. "Fine. They're good."

jobs.title: A draft for the professor
jobs.blurb: Haruka's thesis draft, from the bridge below Ginkaku-ji down the path to a professor who reads at a tea house by the canal.
jobs.to_name: the tea house on the path
jobs.text: Forty pages on pure experience, in a paper folder. "Don't let him see the coffee stain."
jobs.done: The professor finds the coffee stain at once.

jobs.title: The keeper's log book
jobs.blurb: From Mr. Kenji at Nyakuoji, past Eikan-do and Nanzen-ji, to the canal office by the Keage Incline.
jobs.text: A log book of water levels in a careful hand, wrapped in oilcloth. Past the temple and on down to the rails.
jobs.done: "Kenji's book? Tell him his handwriting hasn't improved."

shops.name: Tea house on the path 茶房
shops.where: By the canal, the middle of the path
shops.hello: おこしやす. A seat by the window? The canal is free.

menu.name: Warabi mochi
menu.text: Cold, trembling squares rolled in roasted soybean flour, with black sugar syrup. The starch comes from bracken root, when it is the real thing.

menu.name: Matcha
menu.text: Tea from Uji, south of the city, whisked to a froth in a wide bowl. You turn the bowl twice before you drink, so as not to drink from its front.

shops.name: Yudofu by Nanzen-ji 湯豆腐
shops.hello: Welcome. It is only tofu, and it takes a little while.

menu.name: Yudofu
menu.text: Tofu warmed in a clay pot of kombu broth and eaten with a little soy and spring onion. A monks' dish, served outside this gate since the Edo period.

menu.name: Tofu dengaku
menu.text: Slabs of tofu on bamboo skewers, grilled and painted with sweet miso and a leaf of sansho. It comes before the pot.

shops.name: Shops on the lane 銀閣寺参道
shops.hello: Hai, welcome! Have a taste before you go up.

menu.name: Nama yatsuhashi
menu.text: A soft triangle of rice dough scented with cinnamon, folded over red bean. Every school trip to Kyoto takes a box home.

menu.name: A cherry-print tenugui
menu.text: A cotton hand towel printed with petals on water. It will outlast the blossom by about twenty years.

events.title: The path's cherries
events.text: About four hundred cherries along the canal, at their best from late March to early April in most years. The path is not lit: this is a daytime walk.
lines: The trees meet over the water. The first of them were a gift in the early 1920s from the painter Hashimoto Kansetsu and his wife Yone, who lived nearby, and people still call them Kansetsu's cherries.
When they fall, the petals don't sink. They raft down the canal in a slow pink sheet, northwards, towards Ginkaku-ji.

events.title: Honen-in opens its halls
events.native: 法然院 伽藍内特別公開
events.verb: Go in through the thatched gate
events.text: Honen-in's grounds are open every day, but its halls open to visitors for only two weeks a year: 1 to 7 April and 18 to 24 November.
lines: For one week in spring and one in autumn the main hall is open. On the polished black platform before the Amida, the monks lay out twenty-five fresh flowers, one for each bodhisattva who comes with him.
In April they are camellias, set in rows. The rest of the year you see only the gate and the sand, and that is already a great deal.

events.title: Fireflies on the canal
events.native: 哲学の道のゲンジボタル
events.verb: Wait by the water for the fireflies
events.text: From late May to mid-June, Genji fireflies rise over the canal after dark. They are a registered natural monument of Kyoto City.
lines: About eight o'clock the first green light lifts off the bank, slow, and then others answer it, all blinking in time.
The path has no lamps, which is why they are still here. Nobody uses a flash, and people say sorry to each other in whispers.

events.title: Gozan no Okuribi
events.where: Below Daimonji, at the bridge to Ginkaku-ji
events.text: On 16 August at 20:00 five bonfires are lit on the hills round Kyoto to see the ancestors' spirits off. The first, the great 大 of Daimonji, burns on the mountain above this end of the path.
lines: Eight o'clock. On the slope straight above Ginkaku-ji, seventy-five fires of red pine catch one after another and spell 大, great, eighty metres across its first stroke.
You are almost under it here, too close to read it well. The city reads it from the bridges on the Kamo river. Here you get the firelight on the smoke, and the smell of pine.

events.title: Eikan-do's maples by night
events.native: 永観堂 秋の夜間特別拝観
events.verb: Join the queue at Eikan-do's gate
events.text: From early November to early December in most years, Eikan-do opens again after dark, from 17:30, with its maples lit round the pond.
lines: Kyoto has said 'Eikan-do for maples' for a thousand years. About three thousand of them, lit from below, double themselves in the pond.
Inside is an Amida who looks back over his left shoulder, as if to say: Eikan, you're slow. The queue at the gate is long and nobody minds.
